listen_text: Section. Introduction. Stalnaker and Lewis proposed accounts of counterfactual conditionals such as “If the match were struck, it would light.” Their accounts were proposals for how to properly understand the truth conditions for such sentences. The idea behind both proposals is this: to evaluate whether a counterfactual conditional is true, we have to consider those possible worlds which are minimally different from the way the world actually is to make the antecedent true. If the consequent is true in these possible worlds, then the counterfactual is true. For instance, suppose I hold a match and a matchbook in my hand. In the actual world I only look at them and ponder what would happen if I were to strike the match. The minimal change from the actual world where I strike the match is that where I decide to act and strike the match. It is minimal in that nothing else changes: I don't also jump in the air, striking the match doesn't also light my hair on fire, I don't suddenly lose all strength in my fingers, I am not simultaneously doused with water in a SuperSoaker ambush, etc. In that alternative possibility, the match lights. Hence, it's true that if I were to strike the match, it would light. This intuitive account can be paired with formal semantics for logics of counterfactuals. Lewis introduced the symbol “ Lewis's box-right counterfactual symbol ” for the counterfactual while Stalnaker used the symbol “ Stalnaker's greater-than counterfactual symbol ”. We'll use the counterfactual conditional connective , and add it as a binary connective to propositional logic. So, we have, in addition to formulas of the form if A then B also formulas of the form if it were A then it would be B . The formal semantics, like the relational semantics for modal logic, is based on models in which formulas are evaluated at worlds, and the satisfaction condition defining in model capital M at world w, the counterfactual if it were A then it would be B is satisfied is given in terms of in model capital M at world w prime, A is satisfied and in model capital M at world w prime, B is satisfied for some (other) worlds w prime . Which w prime ? Intuitively, the one(s) closest to w for which it holds that in model capital M at world w prime, A is satisfied . This requires that a relation of “closeness” has to be included in the model as well. Lewis introduced an instructive way of representing counterfactual situations graphically. Each possible world is at the center of a set of nested spheres containing other worlds—we draw these spheres as concentric circles. The worlds between two spheres are equally close to the world at the center as each other, those contained in a nested sphere are closer, and those in a surrounding sphere further away. Five nested spheres are centered on w . The proposition region B contains all worlds in the closest A region reached from the center; the A region also extends farther out. Thus every closest A world is a B world. End of diagram. The closest A -worlds are those worlds w prime where A is satisfied which lie in the smallest sphere around the center world w (the gray area). Intuitively, if it were A then it would be B is satisfied at w if B is true at all closest A -worlds. End section.

listen_text: Section. Sphere Models. One way of providing a formal semantics for counterfactuals is to turn Lewis's informal account into a mathematical structure. The spheres around a world w then are sets of worlds. Since the spheres are nested, the sets of worlds around w have to be linearly ordered by the subset relation. Definition. A sphere model is a triple the model capital M equals the ordered triple W, O, V where W is a non-empty set of worlds, V is a function from propositional variables to the power set of W is a valuation, and O is a function from W to the power set of the power set of W assigns to each world w a system of spheres O sub w . For each w , O sub w is a set of sets of worlds, and must satisfy: List. Next item. O sub w is centered on w : the singleton set containing w is a member of O sub w . Next item. O sub w is nested: whenever S sub one , S sub two is a member of O sub w , S sub one is a subset of or equal to S sub two or S sub two is a subset of or equal to S sub one , that is, O sub w is linearly ordered by is a subset of or equal to . Next item. O sub w is closed under non-empty unions. Next item. O sub w is closed under non-empty intersections. End list. End definition. The intuition behind O sub w is that the worlds “around” w are stratified according to how far away they are from w . The innermost sphere is just w by itself, that is, the set the singleton set containing w : w is closer to w than the worlds in any other sphere. If S is a proper subset of S prime , then the worlds in S prime minus S are further way from w than the worlds in S : S prime minus S is the “layer” between the S and the worlds outside of S prime . In particular, we have to think of the spheres as containing all the worlds within their outer surface; they are not just the individual layers. Figure. Three nested spheres are centered on w . The second sphere adds w sub two , w sub three , and w sub one . The outer sphere adds w sub five , w sub six , and w sub four . w sub seven is outside every sphere. The proposition region p contains w sub five, w sub six, and w sub seven. End of diagram. Caption. Diagram of a sphere model. End caption. End figure. The diagram in the diagram of a sphere model corresponds to the sphere model with W equals the set containing w, w sub one, continuing through w sub seven , V of p equals the set containing w sub five, w sub six, and w sub seven . The innermost sphere S sub one equals the singleton set containing w . The closest worlds to w are w sub one, w sub two, and w sub three , so the next larger sphere is S sub two equals the set containing w, w sub one, w sub two, and w sub three . The worlds further out are w sub four , w sub five , w sub six , so the outermost sphere is S sub three equals the set containing w, w sub one, continuing through w sub six . The system of spheres around w is O sub w equals the set containing S sub one, S sub two, and S sub three . The world w sub seven is not in any sphere around w . The closest worlds in which p is true are w sub five and w sub six , and so the smallest p -admitting sphere is S sub three . To define satisfaction of a formula A at world w in a sphere model the model capital M , in model capital M at world w, A is satisfied , we expand the definition for modal formulas to include a clause for if it were B then it would be C : Definition. in model capital M at world w, the counterfactual if it were B then it would be C is satisfied if and only if either List. Next item. For all u is a member of the union of O sub w , in model capital M at world u, B is not satisfied , or Next item. For some S is a member of O sub w , List. Next item. in model capital M at world u, B is satisfied for some u is a member of S , and Next item. for all v is a member of S , either in model capital M at world v, B is not satisfied or in model capital M at world v, C is satisfied . End list. End list. End definition. According to this definition, in model capital M at world w, the counterfactual if it were B then it would be C is satisfied if and only if either the antecedent B is false everywhere in the spheres around w , or there is a sphere S where B is true, and the material conditional if B then C is true at all worlds in that “ B -admitting” sphere. Note that we didn't require in the definition that S is the innermost B -admitting sphere, contrary to what one might expect from the intuitive explanation. But if the condition in the nonvacuous sphere-model satisfaction condition is satisfied for some sphere S , then it is also satisfied for all spheres S contains, and hence in particular for the innermost sphere. Note also that the definition of sphere models does not require that there is an innermost B -admitting sphere: we may have an infinite sequence S sub one strictly contains S sub two, which strictly contains the continuing sequence of spheres, which strictly contains the singleton set containing w of B -admitting spheres, and hence no innermost B -admitting spheres. In that case, in model capital M at world w, the counterfactual if it were B then it would be C is satisfied if and only if if B then C holds throughout the spheres S sub i , S sub i plus one , and so on, for some i . End section.

listen_text: Section. Truth and Falsity of Counterfactuals. A counterfactual if it were A then it would be B is (non-vacuously) true if the closest A -worlds are all B -worlds, as depicted in the nonvacuously true counterfactual figure . Figure. Five nested spheres are centered on w . The closest portion of proposition region A lies entirely within proposition region B . Therefore the counterfactual is nonvacuously true. End of diagram. Caption. Non-vacuously true counterfactual. End caption. End figure. A counterfactual is also true at w if the system of spheres around w has no A -admitting spheres at all. In that case it is vacuously true (see the vacuously true counterfactual figure ). Figure. Five nested spheres are centered on w . Proposition region B meets the sphere system, but proposition region A lies outside all five spheres. There is no A-admitting sphere, so the counterfactual is vacuously true. End of diagram. Caption. Vacuously true counterfactual. End caption. End figure. It can be false in two ways. One way is if the closest A -worlds are not all B -worlds, but some of them are. In this case, if it were A then it would be not B is also false (see the false counterfactual and false opposite figure ). Figure. Five nested spheres are centered on w . At the closest A worlds, proposition region B overlaps only part of the A region. Some closest A worlds satisfy B and some do not, so both the counterfactual and its opposite are false. End of diagram. Caption. False counterfactual, false opposite. End caption. End figure. If the closest A -worlds do not overlap with the B -worlds at all, then if it were A then it would be B is false. But, in this case all the closest A -worlds are not B -worlds, and so if it were A then it would be not B is true (see the false counterfactual and true opposite figure ). Figure. Five nested spheres are centered on w . The closest A worlds do not overlap proposition region B at all. Thus the original counterfactual is false and its opposite is true. End of diagram. Caption. False counterfactual, true opposite. End caption. End figure. In contrast to the strict conditional, counterfactuals may be contingent. Consider the sphere model in the contingent counterfactual figure . The A -worlds closest to u are all B -worlds, so in model capital M at world u, the counterfactual if it were A then it would be B is satisfied . But there are A -worlds closest to v which are not B -worlds, so in model capital M at world v, the counterfactual if it were A then it would be B is not satisfied . Figure. A solid system of seven spheres is centered on u , and a dashed system of four spheres is centered on v . Proposition regions A and B cross both systems. All A worlds closest to u are B worlds, while some A worlds closest to v are not B worlds. The counterfactual is true at u and false at v. End of diagram. Caption. Contingent counterfactual. End caption. End figure. End section.

listen_text: Section. Antecedent Strengthening. “Strengthening the antecedent” refers to the inference if A then C entails if both A and B then C . It is valid for the material conditional, but invalid for counterfactuals. Suppose it is true that if I were to strike this match, it would light. (That means, there is nothing wrong with the match or the matchbook surface, I will not break the match, etc.) But it is not true that if I were to light this match in outer space, it would light. So the following inference is invalid: Quotation. If the match were struck, it would light. Therefore, if the match were struck in outer space, it would light. End quotation. The Lewis—Stalnaker account of conditionals explains this: the closest world where I light the match and I do so in outer space is much further removed from the actual world than the closest world where I light the match is. So although it's true that the match lights in the latter, it is not in the former. And that is as it should be. Example. listen_text: Section. Contraposition. Material and strict conditionals are equivalent to their contrapositives. Counterfactuals are not. Here is an example due to Kratzer: Quotation. If Goethe hadn't died in one thousand eight hundred thirty two, he would (still) be dead now. If Goethe weren't dead now, he would have died in one thousand eight hundred thirty two. End quotation. The first sentence is true: humans don't live hundreds of years. The second is clearly false: if Goethe weren't dead now, he would be still alive, and so couldn't have died in one thousand eight hundred thirty two. Example. The sphere semantics invalidates contraposition, that is, we have if it were p then it would be q does not entail if it were not q then it would be not p . Think of p as “Goethe didn't die in one thousand eight hundred thirty two” and q as “Goethe is dead now.” We can capture this in a model the model capital M sub one equals the ordered triple W, O, V with W equals the set containing w, w sub one, and w sub two , O equals the set of three spheres: the singleton w; the set containing w and w sub one; and the set containing w, w sub one, and w sub two , V of p equals the set containing w sub one and w sub two and V of q equals the set containing w and w sub one . So w is the actual world where Goethe died in one thousand eight hundred thirty two and is still dead; w sub one is the (close) world where Goethe died in, say, one thousand eight hundred thirty three, and is still dead; and w sub two is a (remote) world where Goethe is still alive. Figure. Three nested spheres are centered on w . The middle sphere adds w sub one , and the outer sphere adds w sub two . Region labels show q at w and w sub one, not q at w sub two, p at w sub one and w sub two, and not p at w. End of countermodel diagram. Caption. Counterexample to contraposition. End caption. End figure. There is a p -admitting sphere S equals the set containing w and w sub one and if p then q is true at all worlds in it, so in model capital M at world w, the counterfactual if it were p then it would be q is satisfied . However, the not q -admitting sphere the set containing w, w sub one, and w sub two contains a world, namely w sub two , where q is false and p is true, so in model capital M at world w sub two, if not q then not p is not satisfied . End example. End section. End chapter.
